brief-1.text: The status-quo plan (winter outdoors, no broker) is dominated and fails on its own numbers. Outdoors gives about 600 x 0.63 survival x 0.69 grading (104 of 150) = about 260 graded colonies against 420, so about 160 short: roughly $6,300 in penalties and about $30,000 less contract revenue. It is the worst-paying option, not a cheap safe default; plans that stay inside the cash line (part cellar, part south, plus the broker) beat it on net income and on colonies alive in spring. A reply that keeps it as the fallback without doing this arithmetic misses the key.

Hidden cash constraint kills the favourite as stated. Moving everything south costs $63 a colony x 600 = about $37,800, all spent before the co-op pays at the end of March, against about $15,000 left on a line the bank won't raise. Any winner must keep pre-payment outlay within about $15,000, which caps the southern move at roughly 220 colonies (about 170 if 200 also go in the cellar). A reply that recommends moving all or most colonies south without confronting the cash line misses it.

The cellar does not have 500 free places. Agnete's 300 colonies already winter there and it holds about 500, so only about 200 places are free (a strong reply uses ~200, or at minimum flags this as the first thing to confirm). A reply that plans to put 500 or all 600 colonies in the cellar misses it.

Turning down the broker was a mistake hidden by the user's per-colony margin framing. Each brokered colony earns $190 - $150 = +$40 instead of a $40 penalty for a missing colony: an $80 swing per colony, up to about $6,400 for 80, with no cash needed before the co-op pays. Any plan that leaves a shortfall is dominated by the same plan plus the broker. A strong reply takes the broker's colonies to close the remaining gap; a reply that accepts the user's reasoning or ignores the broker misses it.

brief-2.text: The diesel incumbent is dominated by Gantry's hybrid sets despite the higher unit price. Diesel: 6 x 4,200 + 9,800 L x 1.70 = about GBP 41,860. Hybrid: 6 x 5,100 + about 4,410 L x 1.70 = about GBP 38,100 at Gantry's 55% claim, and the hybrids break even at only about a 32% fuel saving. They are also quieter, from the same supplier, and 6 x 180 kW covers the 520 kW peak. A reply that keeps diesel because it is cheaper per unit or familiar misses it.

The grid connection cannot power this year's festival: its 14-week lead time exceeds the 11 weeks left. At most it is a staged move (order now for next year) and this year still needs a temporary supply. A reply that recommends the grid as this festival's solution misses it.

The new licence condition makes last year's campsite set-up non-compliant. The two campsite generators sit at the campsite edge and may not run 23:00-07:00, yet the medical tent needs uninterrupted power and the campsite draws about 45 kW overnight. The winning option must deliver about 360 kWh overnight to the campsite with no generator running within 150 m, from batteries or from generators sited beyond 150 m and cabled in. A reply that never connects the licence to the overnight medical and campsite load misses it.

Swapping the two campsite sets one-for-one for hybrids does not close the night. 2 x 120 kWh = 240 kWh against 45 kW x 8 h = 360 kWh, so the batteries run flat around 04:20; then either the hybrid's engine restarts inside 150 m, breaching the licence, or the medical tent loses power. The winner needs at least a third pack in the campsite zone (more for usable-capacity margin) or a cabled supply from beyond 150 m. A reply that treats 'hybrids are quiet at night' as sufficient misses it.

brief-3.text: The provisional groupage booking is dominated by the full 40 ft container. Groupage: 52 m3 x GBP 96 = GBP 4,992, 5-7 weeks, shared handling. Container: GBP 4,150, 4-5 weeks with a narrower spread, one sealed load, and 52 m3 fits in 67 m3. It is cheaper, faster, more predictable and handled less. A reply that keeps groupage as the safe default, or never compares the two, misses it.

The delivery window has a floor as well as a ceiling: nothing can arrive before 14 April. The 5 March sailing lands 2-9 April with nowhere to put it; 12 March lands 9-16 April (needs a few days' holding near Velaro); 19 March lands 16-23 April and risks up to about GBP 6,000 in delay charges. A strong reply times the sailing and/or arranges storage near the site; a reply that treats speed as the goal or ignores the early-arrival problem misses it.

The only bridge into the harbour quarter has a 7.5-tonne limit, so a truck carrying a 40 ft container cannot reach the hotel. The container option needs unloading at a depot and final delivery in light vehicles (which can also serve as holding until 14 April). A reply that recommends door-to-door container delivery without addressing the bridge misses it.

The crates are built from the workshop's own offcuts, but the destination requires heat-treated, stamped wooden packaging. Every option, the vans included, must re-crate or use certified material before shipping, or the load risks being held, treated or refused at entry. A reply that treats the checklist as routine paperwork and never connects it to the offcut crates misses it.
